source: built-in example (heterogeneity/index.html EXAMPLE: 8 trials, log odds ratios), default options: Paule-Mandel tau2
plain: This analysis combined 8 studies. On the scale on which the study effects were entered, the average effect was estimated at −0.207. Allowing for chance, the true average effect is likely to lie in the range −0.388 to −0.025 (95% confidence interval). If zero means no effect on this scale (differences or log ratios), this interval excludes no effect. The amount of variation between the studies’ results beyond what chance would explain may represent substantial heterogeneity (I² = 62.8%); the estimated variance of the true effects across studies (τ²) was 0.0294. In a new setting similar to these studies, the true effect could plausibly be anywhere from −0.651 to 0.237. This summary describes the included studies; it does not show what causes the differences between them or whether the effect matters to patients.
methods: Study effect estimates and their standard errors were combined, on the scale on which they were entered, in an inverse-variance random-effects model. The between-study variance (τ²) was estimated with the Paule–Mandel estimator (Paule and Mandel 1982). The pooled estimate is reported with two 95% confidence intervals (CIs): a normal (Wald, z) interval, and a modified Hartung–Knapp interval (Hartung and Knapp 2001) in which the variance of the pooled estimate is multiplied by the weighted residual variance of the studies, truncated below at one, with critical values from a t distribution with the number of studies minus one degrees of freedom. Heterogeneity was summarised with Cochran’s Q (common-effect weights; P value from the chi-squared distribution with the number of studies minus one degrees of freedom), with I² computed from Q as (Q − df)/Q, expressed as a percentage and truncated at zero, and with a model-based I² computed as τ²/(τ² + s²), where s² is the typical within-study variance (Higgins and Thompson 2002). I² was interpreted with the overlapping bands given in Cochrane Handbook v6.5, §10.10.2. A 95% CI for τ² was obtained with the Q-profile method (the generalised Q statistic profiled against chi-squared quantiles; it does not depend on the chosen τ² estimator) and transformed into a CI for the model-based I² through s². Paule–Mandel and REML estimates of τ² are also reported for comparison. A 95% prediction interval was computed as the pooled estimate ± t × √(τ² + SE²), where SE is the unadjusted standard error of the pooled estimate and t comes from a t distribution with the number of studies minus one degrees of freedom (Cochrane Handbook v6.5, §10.10.4.3; Higgins, Thompson and Spiegelhalter 2009); it is reported when at least 3 studies are available. Influence was explored with leave-one-out re-analyses, re-estimating τ² with the same estimator in each subset, and with a Baujat plot of each study’s squared Pearson residual at the fitted τ² against its influence on the pooled estimate (the squared change in the pooled estimate when the study is omitted, divided by the variance of the leave-one-out estimate). Analyses were run in allmeta heterogeneity <build.version> (commit <build.shortSha>).
results: The analysis included 8 studies. The random-effects pooled estimate was −0.207 (95% CI −0.388 to −0.025 with the modified Hartung–Knapp method; −0.357 to −0.056 with the normal approximation), using τ² = 0.0294 (Paule–Mandel). Cochran’s Q = 18.82 (df = 7, p = 0.009); I² = 62.8% (Q-based; Cochrane Handbook v6.5, §10.10.2: may represent substantial heterogeneity); model-based I² = 65.1% (95% CI 15.1% to 92.3%, Q-profile). The 95% Q-profile CI for τ² was 0.0028 to 0.1872. Other estimates of τ² were Paule–Mandel 0.0294 and REML 0.0279. The 95% prediction interval for the effect in a new study similar to those included was −0.651 to 0.237.
flags: The Q-based I² and the model-based I² are different quantities and can differ; the Q-profile interval refers to the model-based I².
references: Paule RC, Mandel J. Consensus values and weighting factors. J Res Natl Bur Stand 1982;87:377-385.
Hartung J, Knapp G. A refined method for the meta-analysis of controlled clinical trials with binary outcome. Stat Med 2001;20:3875-3889.
Higgins JPT, Thompson SG. Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Stat Med 2002;21:1539-1558.
